s: Fehling's solution is reduced by aliphatic aldehydes, giving a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide.
Of the choices, only C₂H₅CHO (propanal) is an aldehyde; it has no –OH group, so it does not react with sodium. The alcohols react with Na; acetone does not reduce Fehling's.
mcqs.n: Fehling's test gives cuprous oxide, Cu₂O (red), not cupric oxide as printed.

shortQuestions: In an aldehyde the carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen atom (–CHO group, at the end of a chain), e.g. CH₃CHO.
In a ketone the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon groups (>C=O within the chain), e.g. CH₃COCH₃. Because of the C–H bond, aldehydes are easily oxidised (reducing agents) while ketones are not.
The acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen: R₂C=O + H⁺ ⇌ R₂C=OH⁺.
The positive charge is shared with the carbon (R₂C⁺–OH), so the carbonyl carbon becomes more electron-deficient (more electrophilic) and even weak nucleophiles (H₂O, ROH) can attack it.
The C=O bond is polar: oxygen is much more electronegative, so the carbon carries a partial positive charge and is attacked by nucleophiles; the oxygen then takes the negative charge.
The C=C bond is non-polar; its exposed π electron cloud is electron-rich and attracts electrophiles. Hence carbonyl compounds undergo nucleophilic addition and alkenes electrophilic addition.

An aldehyde has a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon; this C–H bond is easily oxidised to C–OH, giving a carboxylic acid with the same number of carbons (even mild oxidants like Tollens' and Fehling's reagents do this).
A ketone has no such hydrogen; oxidation requires breaking a strong C–C bond, which needs strong oxidising agents and drastic conditions.
Hydration: an acid makes the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic, and a base supplies the stronger nucleophile OH⁻ — either speeds up the reaction.

Addition of HCN: the real nucleophile is CN⁻. HCN is a weak acid; a base increases [CN⁻] (HCN + OH⁻ → CN⁻ + H₂O), whereas acid suppresses its ionisation and lowers [CN⁻]. So only base catalyses cyanohydrin formation.
In a Grignard reagent the C–Mg bond is highly polar, so the alkyl group acts as a very strong nucleophile (a carbanion source) that attacks the carbonyl carbon directly.
At the same time Mg²⁺ acts as a Lewis acid by coordinating to the carbonyl oxygen, activating it. So no additional catalyst is needed (the reaction is done in dry ether).
A ketone has two alkyl groups on the carbonyl carbon, an aldehyde only one (or none).

Electronic effect: alkyl groups donate electrons (+I), reducing the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon. Steric effect: two alkyl groups crowd the carbon and hinder the approach of the nucleophile. So ketones are less reactive than aldehydes.
The carbonyl oxygen has lone pairs and a partial negative charge, so it accepts hydrogen bonds from water molecules (C=O···H–O–H).
Lower aldehydes and ketones (formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, acetone) are small, so this hydrogen bonding makes them very soluble; solubility decreases as the hydrocarbon part grows.
Ketones are oxidised only by strong oxidants, which break a C–C bond next to the carbonyl group.
The carbon chain is split into two parts, so each carboxylic acid formed contains fewer carbon atoms than the parent ketone (e.g. CH₃COCH₂CH₃ gives CH₃COOH + CH₃COOH, or HCOOH + CH₃CH₂COOH).

Tollens' test: warm the compound with Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺). An aldehyde reduces Ag⁺ to metallic silver, which forms a shining silver mirror on the tube: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2Ag + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O.
Ketones give no mirror. (Fehling's test: aliphatic aldehydes give a brick-red Cu₂O precipitate; ketones do not.)
longQuestions: Ketones: CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃ (pentan-2-one); CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ (pentan-3-one); CH₃COCH(CH₃)₂ (3-methylbutan-2-one). In all, seven carbonyl isomers (2-methylbutanal is also chiral).

(b) Structure: the carbonyl carbon is sp²-hybridised; it forms three σ bonds in one plane at about 120° and a π bond with oxygen by sideways overlap of p orbitals. Oxygen is more electronegative, so the C=O bond is polar: Cδ+=Oδ−.

Reactivity: the electrophilic carbon is attacked by nucleophiles (nucleophilic addition of HCN, NaHSO₃, Grignard reagents, alcohols, ammonia derivatives); the oxygen can be protonated (acid catalysis). The polar C=O also makes α-hydrogens acidic (enolisation, aldol condensation). Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones for electronic and steric reasons.

(a) i. Cyanohydrin: CH₃CHO + HCN —base→ CH₃CH(OH)CN. ii. Oxime: CH₃CHO + NH₂OH → CH₃CH=NOH + H₂O. iii. Imine (Schiff base): CH₃CHO + CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CH=NCH₃ + H₂O. iv. Hydrazone: (CH₃)₂C=O + NH₂NH₂ → (CH₃)₂C=NNH₂ + H₂O. v. Acetal: CH₃CHO + 2C₂H₅OH —dry HCl→ CH₃CH(OC₂H₅)₂ + H₂O.
(b) Grignard reagent + carbonyl compound, then hydrolysis (H₃O⁺): i. Butan-1-ol: CH₃CH₂CH₂MgBr + HCHO → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH. ii. Ethyl alcohol: CH₃MgI + HCHO → CH₃CH₂OH.
iii. Butan-2-ol: CH₃CH₂MgBr + CH₃CHO → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ (or CH₃MgI + CH₃CH₂CHO). iv. 2-Methylbutan-2-ol: CH₃CH₂MgBr + CH₃COCH₃ → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃.

(a) Preparation of aldehydes: (i) controlled oxidation of primary alcohols (PCC, or K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ with the aldehyde distilled off): CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O. (ii) Dehydrogenation of primary alcohols over copper at 300 °C: RCH₂OH → RCHO + H₂. (iii) Rosenmund reduction of acid chlorides: RCOCl + H₂ —Pd/BaSO₄→ RCHO + HCl. (Also ozonolysis of alkenes and hydration of acetylene, HC≡CH + H₂O —HgSO₄/H₂SO₄→ CH₃CHO.)

(b) i. With ethylmagnesium iodide, then hydrolysis: CH₃CHO + C₂H₅MgI → CH₃CH(OMgI)C₂H₅ → CH₃CH(OH)C₂H₅ (butan-2-ol). ii. With zinc–mercury amalgam in HCl (Clemmensen reduction): CH₃CHO + 4[H] → CH₃CH₃ + H₂O (ethane).
iii. With lithium aluminium hydride: CH₃CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol). iv. With acidified dichromate: CH₃CHO + [O] → CH₃COOH (acetic acid); the orange solution turns green (Cr³⁺).

(a) Friedel–Crafts acylation: benzene reacts with an acyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃: C₆H₆ + CH₃COCl → C₆H₅COCH₃ (acetophenone) + HCl. AlCl₃ forms the acylium ion: CH₃COCl + AlCl₃ → CH₃C≡O⁺ + AlCl₄⁻; the electrophile attacks the ring to give an arenium ion, which loses H⁺ (taken by AlCl₄⁻, regenerating AlCl₃). With benzoyl chloride, benzophenone C₆H₅COC₆H₅ is formed.

(b) From acetone: i. Propane — Clemmensen reduction: CH₃COCH₃ + 4[H] —Zn–Hg/HCl→ CH₃CH₂CH₃ + H₂O. ii. Propan-2-ol — reduction with NaBH₄, LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni: CH₃COCH₃ + 2[H] → (CH₃)₂CHOH. iii. Acetone cyanohydrin — HCN with a little base: (CH₃)₂CO + HCN → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN.

iv. Acetone hydrazone — with hydrazine: (CH₃)₂CO + NH₂NH₂ → (CH₃)₂C=NNH₂ + H₂O. v. Acetic acid — haloform reaction with NaOI (I₂/NaOH): CH₃COCH₃ + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CH₃COONa + CHI₃ + 3NaI + 3H₂O, then acidify to CH₃COOH (or vigorous oxidation with K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, which cleaves the molecule).

(a) Base-catalysed nucleophilic addition: the base produces a strong nucleophile (e.g. HCN + OH⁻ → CN⁻); the nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon, the π electrons move to oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide ion; the alkoxide takes a proton from the solvent or HCN, giving the product (cyanohydrin) and regenerating the nucleophile. Acid-catalysed: H⁺ protonates the carbonyl oxygen, making the carbon strongly electrophilic; a weak nucleophile (H₂O, ROH) attacks the carbon; loss of H⁺ from the attacking group gives the product (hydrate, hemiacetal) and regenerates H⁺.

(b) Physical properties: formaldehyde is a gas; other lower aldehydes and ketones are liquids, higher ones solids. Their boiling points are higher than those of alkanes of similar mass (dipole–dipole attraction) but lower than those of alcohols (no intermolecular hydrogen bonding). Lower members are soluble in water (hydrogen bonding with water). Lower aldehydes have sharp, pungent smells; ketones and higher aldehydes have pleasant smells; acetone is a good solvent.
(c, d) Structural formulas: i. 2,4-dimethylpent-2-enal: OHC–C(CH₃)=CH–CH(CH₃)–CH₃. ii. 2,2-dimethylbutanal: OHC–C(CH₃)₂–CH₂CH₃. iii. 3,3-dimethylhex-4-en-2-one: CH₃CO–C(CH₃)₂–CH=CH–CH₃.
iv. 4-methylhex-5-en-3-one: CH₃CH₂CO–CH(CH₃)–CH=CH₂. v. pent-4-yn-2-one: CH₃CO–CH₂–C≡CH. (Part (c) prints no structures to be named, so only part (d) can be answered.)
activities: Preparing Tollens' reagent: NH₄OH first precipitates brown silver oxide, 2AgNO₃ + 2NH₄OH → Ag₂O + 2NH₄NO₃ + H₂O; excess ammonia dissolves it as the diamminesilver(I) ion, Ag₂O + 4NH₃ + H₂O → 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 2OH⁻.

Glucose contains an aldehyde (–CHO) group, which reduces Ag⁺ to metallic silver while it is oxidised: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2Ag↓ + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O. The silver deposits as a bright mirror on the clean glass.

Conclusion: aldehydes give a silver mirror; ketones (e.g. acetone) give no mirror, so the test distinguishes aldehydes from ketones. Safety: prepare the reagent fresh and wash it away after use, since on standing it can form explosive silver compounds.
